--- title: "Shakespeare's Sonnets" subtitle: "A whole-corpus computational reading: meter, rhyme, ambiguity, and learned weights" jupyter: python3 --- The 1609 Quarto — 154 sonnets, 2,155 lines — is small enough to read and large enough to count. This page does both: every table and figure below is computed by the code shown, on the corpus that ships with Prosodic (`corpora/corppoetry_en/en.shakespeare.txt`). To rerun it yourself, [install Prosodic](../install.qmd) and execute the cells top to bottom; the site itself embeds frozen results (`quarto`'s `freeze`), so what you see is one real execution, not a mock-up. ## Load and parse The parser is exhaustive: for every line it evaluates *every* segmentation into weak/strong positions against the constraint set, then discards candidates that lose under any possible weighting (harmonic bounding — see [Metrical parsing](../methods/metrical-parsing.qmd)). Vectorization makes this affordable: the whole corpus parses in about two seconds on a laptop CPU. ::: {#setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import time, warnings from pathlib import Path warnings.filterwarnings('ignore') import pandas as pd import prosodic # resolve the bundled corpus relative to wherever this page is executed; # fall back to the GitHub copy if run outside a prosodic checkout _rel = Path('corpora') / 'corppoetry_en' / 'en.shakespeare.txt' _root = next((p for p in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents] if (p / _rel).exists()), None) corpus_fn = (str(_root / _rel) if _root else 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quadrismegistus/prosodic' '/master/corpora/corppoetry_en/en.shakespeare.txt') t0 = time.perf_counter() corpus = prosodic.Text(fn=corpus_fn) t1 = time.perf_counter() corpus.parse() t2 = time.perf_counter() print(f"{len(corpus.stanzas)} sonnets, {len(corpus.lines):,} lines") print(f"init {t1-t0:.2f}s parse {t2-t1:.2f}s") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 154 sonnets, 2,155 lines init 1.04s parse 2.06s ``` ::: ::: ## The shape of the corpus Prosodic's form detection aggregates over every line's best parse. Asked what meter this is, it answers like a metrist would: binary feet, final-headed (rising), i.e. **iambic**; five beats and ten syllables per line, invariantly. ::: {#cell-meter-type .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} mt = corpus.meter_type {k: mt[k] for k in ('foot', 'head', 'type')} ``` ::: {#meter-type .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'foot': 'binary', 'head': 'final', 'type': 'iambic'} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#schemes .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} print('feet per line: ', corpus.line_scheme['combo']) print('syllables per line:', corpus.syllable_scheme['combo']) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` feet per line: (5,) syllables per line: (10,) ``` ::: ::: How iambic is iambic? Score each line's best parse (the weighted sum of its constraint violations; 0 = a perfectly alternating pentameter with no mismatch). Most of the corpus sits at 0–2 violations — the meter is real, not a critic's idealization — with a long tail of rougher lines. ::: {#cell-fig-scores .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from plotnine import (aes, element_blank, geom_bar, ggplot, labs, theme, theme_minimal) lines_df = pd.DataFrame({ 'line': [l.txt.strip() for l in corpus.lines], 'score': [l.best_parse.score for l in corpus.lines], 'ambig': [len(l.parses.unbounded) for l in corpus.lines], }) (ggplot(lines_df, aes('factor(score)')) + geom_bar(fill='#2a78d6') + labs(x='best-parse score (weighted constraint violations)', y='lines') + theme_minimal() + theme(panel_grid_major_x=element_blank(), figure_size=(7, 3.2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Distribution of best-parse scores across all 2,155 lines.](sonnets_files/figure-html/fig-scores-output-1.png){#fig-scores width=700 height=320} ::: ::: ## A rhyme census Rhyme detection works from sound, not spelling: feature-weighted edit distance over the IPA of each line's final rime. Classifying each sonnet's rhyme-group pattern against a catalog of 39 named schemes: ::: {#cell-rhyme-census .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} from collections import Counter schemes, strict = Counter(), 0 for st in corpus.stanzas: sonnet = prosodic.Text(st.txt) rs = sonnet.rhyme_scheme schemes[rs['name'] if rs else '(no scheme)'] += 1 strict += bool(sonnet.is_shakespearean_sonnet) pd.DataFrame(schemes.most_common(), columns=['scheme', 'sonnets']) ``` ::: {#rhyme-census .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
scheme sonnets
0 Sonnet, Shakespearean 137
1 Sonnet A 4
2 Sonnet D 3
3 Sonnet C 3
4 Sonnet, Spenserian 2
5 Rhyme Royal 2
6 Sonnet B 1
7 Alternating D 1
8 Couplet 1
``` ::: ::: ::: {#strict-count .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(f"{strict}/154 pass the strict is_shakespearean_sonnet predicate") print(f"(14 lines, ~10 syllables, and best-matching scheme = abab cdcd efef gg)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 136/154 pass the strict is_shakespearean_sonnet predicate (14 lines, ~10 syllables, and best-matching scheme = abab cdcd efef gg) ``` ::: ::: The 137 that classify as Shakespearean are unsurprising — Shakespeare mostly wrote Shakespearean sonnets. The residue is where it gets interesting. Sonnet 126 ("O thou, my lovely boy") really *isn't* one — the detector reads its twelve lines as `aabbccddeeff` and files it under **Couplet**, which is what it is. And Sonnet 106 classifies as **Sonnet A** rather than Shakespearean: ::: {#sonnet-106 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from prosodic.analysis import nums_to_scheme s106 = prosodic.Text(corpus.stanzas[105].txt) print('detected:', ''.join(nums_to_scheme(s106.rhyme_ids)), '->', s106.rhyme_scheme['name'], f"({s106.rhyme_scheme['form']})") print('line-final words:') print(' ', ', '.join(l.txt.strip().split()[-1].strip(',;:.') for l in s106.lines)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` detected: abab-c-c-dedee -> Sonnet A (abab cdcd eefeff) line-final words: time, wights, rhyme, knights, best, brow, express'd, now, prophecies, prefiguring, eyes, sing, days, praise ``` ::: ::: The quatrains open cleanly (*time/rhyme*, *wights/knights*), but the third quatrain rhymes *prophecies/eyes* and *prefiguring/sing* — slant rhymes to a modern ear and to the phonetic distance measure alike. With those edges missing, the nearest named scheme is a sonnet variant with a different sestet. This is expected behavior worth keeping: the classifier reports what the sounds support, and disagreements with the print tradition mark exactly the lines where pronunciation has drifted since 1609. ## Close reading: Sonnet 18 `summary()` gives the per-line scansion, rhyme letter, and ambiguity count, plus the estimated schema: ::: {#sonnet-18 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} s18 = prosodic.Text(corpus.stanzas[17].txt) s18.parse() print(s18.summary()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #st #ln parse rhyme #feet #syll #parse ----- ----- ----------- ------- ------- ------- -------- 1 1 -+-+-+-+-+ a 5 10 1 1 2 -+-+-+-+- - 4 9 1 1 3 -+-+-+-+-- a 4 10 2 1 4 -+-+--++-+ - 4 10 2 1 5 -+-+-+-+-+ b 5 9 3 1 6 -+-+-+-+-+ c 5 10 2 1 7 -+-+-+-+-+ b 5 10 1 1 8 -+-+-+-+-+ c 5 10 1 1 9 -+-+-+-+-+ d 5 10 1 1 10 -+-+-+-+-+- e 5 11 2 1 11 --++-+-+-+ d 4 10 2 1 12 -+-+-+-+-+- e 5 11 1 1 13 -+-+-+-+-+ f 5 10 1 1 14 -+-+--++-- f 3 10 6 estimated schema ---------- meter: Iambic feet: Complex (5-4-4-4-5-5-3) syllables: 10 rhyme: Sonnet, Shakespearean (abab cdcd efefgg) ``` ::: ::: For individual lines, `grid_str()` renders the best parse as a Hayes-style metrical grid: column height is linguistic prominence, and the `w`/`s` row beneath is the metrical template, so a mismatch reads as a tall column over a `w` (positions with violations are starred). The famous opening line is metrically docile — every strong position is at least as prominent as its neighbors: ::: {#grid-l1 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(s18.line1.grid_str()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * shall I com PARE thee TO a SUM mer's DAY w s* w s w s* w s w s ``` ::: ::: Line 3 is not. *Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May* opens with a stressed monosyllable in the first weak position — the `w*` under *rough*: ::: {#grid-l3 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} line3 = s18.lines[2] print(line3.txt.strip()) print() print(line3.grid_str()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May, * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * rough WINDS do SHAKE the DAR ling BUDS of may w* s w s w s w s w w ``` ::: ::: Hold that thought: the tolerance of line-initial stress is exactly what the weight-learning experiment below will discover on its own. ## Metrical ambiguity A line's `parses.unbounded` are its Pareto-optimal scansions — readings that survive harmonic bounding. Most lines have one or two; a few monosyllable-heavy lines support many more. The most ambiguous lines in the corpus: ::: {#cell-most-ambiguous .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} lines_df.sort_values('ambig', ascending=False).head(5)[['ambig', 'score', 'line']] ``` ::: {#most-ambiguous .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
ambig score line
1449 18 4.0 Three April perfumes in three hot Junes burn'd,
1891 17 4.0 And will, thy soul knows, is admitted there;
1321 16 3.0 Making lascivious comments on thy sport,
129 15 3.0 But that thou none lovest is most evident;
451 14 3.0 Gilding pale streams with heavenly alchemy;
``` ::: ::: The champion — 18 defensible scansions — is from Sonnet 104, a line made almost entirely of stressable monosyllables: ::: {#cell-scansion-table .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} champ = max(corpus.lines, key=lambda l: len(l.parses.unbounded)) print(champ.txt.strip()) def scansion_row(p): row = {'meter': p.meter_str, 'score': p.score, 'bounded': p.is_bounded} row.update({'*' + k: v for k, v in sorted(p.viold.items()) if v}) return row pd.DataFrame( [scansion_row(p) for p in champ.parses.unbounded] + [scansion_row(p) for p in list(champ.parses.bounded)[:3]] ).fillna(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Three April perfumes in three hot Junes burn'd, ``` ::: ::: {#scansion-table .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The bounded rows at the bottom show what bounding removes. Compare the first bounded scansion with the first unbounded one: ::: {#bounding-demo .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} ub, bd = champ.parses.unbounded[0], champ.parses.bounded[0] for tag, p in [('unbounded', ub), ('bounded ', bd)]: viols = {k: v for k, v in p.viold.items() if v} print(f"{tag} {p.meter_str} score={p.score} {viols}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` unbounded ++--+-++-+ score=4.0 {'unres_across': 3, 'w_stress': 1} bounded ++--+--+-+ score=5.0 {'unres_across': 3, 'w_stress': 2} ``` ::: ::: The bounded parse incurs everything the unbounded one does *plus* an extra `w_stress` violation: no weighting of the constraints could ever prefer it. That is [harmonic bounding](../methods/metrical-parsing.qmd#the-model) — the parser keeps these candidates (the web app's Line view shows them grayed out) but they can never win. ## Learning the meter's weights So far every constraint has counted equally. `Meter.fit()` learns weights from the corpus itself by Maximum-Entropy optimization: make the observed scansion (here, a uniform iambic-pentameter target) as probable as possible against each line's full candidate set. With `zones=3` the violation tensor is split into line-initial, medial, and final thirds, so the model can learn *positional* leniency: ::: {#cell-maxent .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} meter = prosodic.Meter() meter.fit(corpus, 'wswswswsws', zones=3) zw = meter.zone_weights base_names = sorted({n.rsplit('_z', 1)[0] for n in zw}) weights = pd.DataFrame( [{'constraint': b, **{f'zone {z}': round(zw.get(f'{b}_z{z}', 0.0), 2) for z in (1, 2, 3)}} for b in base_names] ).set_index('constraint') weights ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [6.84s] prosodic.parsing.maxent.MaxEntTrainer._build_line_data(): 438/2155 lines had no matching scansion among parser candidates (syllable count mismatch?) ``` ::: ::: {#maxent .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
zone 1 zone 2 zone 3
constraint
foot_size 0.00 0.00 0.00
s_unstress 0.44 0.00 0.00
unres_across 9.81 9.97 10.17
unres_within 8.04 8.75 8.93
w_peak 0.89 1.17 1.14
w_stress 0.00 1.97 1.70
``` ::: ::: Two things the model discovers match the metrist's textbook: - **Resolution is the hard currency.** The `unres_*` constraints (splitting a two-syllable position across a word boundary or inside a strong/heavy disyllable) carry the largest weights everywhere — these are the near-inviolable rules of the iambic pentameter template. - **Line-initial inversion is free.** `w_stress` — stress in weak position — costs ~2 in the middle and end of the line but **0 in zone 1**. The model has independently learned the license that put *Rough winds* in line 3 above: a stressed syllable in the opening weak position simply isn't penalized in Shakespeare's practice. (Kiparsky's stricter `w_peak`, a lexical stress *maximum* in weak position, stays costly in all zones.) ## Finale: phrasal stress Everything above used lexical stress. With `syntax=True`, Prosodic also computes *sentence-level* prominence from a dependency parse — Dozat's MetricalTree algorithm, ported to spaCy projections (see [Phrasal stress](../methods/phrasal-stress.qmd); requires `pip install "prosodic[syntax]"`). Each word gets gradient `pstress` and `tstress` values in [0, 1], where `tstress = 1.0` is the sentence's **nuclear stress**: ::: {#cell-phrasal .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} s18x = prosodic.Text(corpus.stanzas[17].txt, syntax=True) s18x.parse() df = s18x.df (df[(df.line_num == 1) & (df.form_idx == 0)] .drop_duplicates('word_num')[['word_txt', 'pstress', 'tstress']] .set_index('word_txt').T) ``` ::: {#phrasal .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}
word_txt Shall I compare thee to a summer's day
pstress 0.0 0.333333 0.0 0.333333 0.0 0.0 0.0 1.0
tstress 0.285714 0.0 0.571429 0.0 0.285714 0.142857 0.571429 1.0
``` ::: ::: The grid consumes these values: phrasal rows extend the columns *above* the word level, so the nuclear-stress word — *day*, the point of the question — becomes the tallest column: ::: {#grid-phrasal .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(s18x.line1.grid_str()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * shall I com PARE thee TO a SUM mer's DAY w s* w s w s* w s w s ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-grid-plot .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} from plotnine import theme s18x.line1.grid_plot() + theme(figure_size=(8, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The same grid as a figure: `line.grid_plot()` (plotnine).](sonnets_files/figure-html/fig-grid-plot-output-1.png){#fig-grid-plot width=800 height=300} ::: ::: Gradient prominence also feeds the parser: the constraints `w_stress_p` / `s_unstress_p` and `w_stress_t` / `s_unstress_t` penalize phrasally prominent syllables in weak positions (and weak ones in strong) — inert without `syntax=True`, and most useful for prose rhythm and naturalness ranking rather than fixed-template verse. ## Reproducing this page Everything here runs from a stock install: ```sh pip install prosodic # + espeak (see Install) ``` Related reading: [Metrical parsing](../methods/metrical-parsing.qmd) for the theory and the vectorized implementation · [Phrasal stress](../methods/phrasal-stress.qmd) for the MetricalTree lineage · the [README notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/github/quadrismegistus/prosodic/blob/master/README.ipynb) for a runnable API tour.
